Ensembling machine learning models improves performance, but deploying heavy ensembles is computationally expensive [P3_p1_c02]. This paper solves the deployment problem by transferring knowledge from a cumbersome model or ensemble into a single, compact model suitable for deployment, using a process called distillation [P3_p1_c03]. 

While training requires heavy computation to extract structure from large datasets, deployment has strict latency and resource constraints [P3_p1_c03]. A conceptual block in knowledge transfer is identifying knowledge strictly with learned parameter values [P3_p1_c04]. Distillation instead treats knowledge more abstractly [P3_p1_c04]. For tasks like MNIST, soft targets contain valuable information in the ratios of small probabilities, defining a rich similarity structure over the data [P3_p2_c04]. Caruana and collaborators used logits by minimizing the squared difference between cumbersome and small models [P3_p2_c04]. The authors' more general distillation solution raises the temperature of the final softmax to produce soft targets, and uses that same high temperature when training the small model [P3_p2_c04]. Matching logits is a special case of this approach [P3_p2_c04].

The authors also introduce ensembles composed of full models and specialist models targeting fine-grained classes [P3_p1_c02]. Specialists are clustered using an on-line K-means algorithm applied to the covariance matrix of generalist predictions [P3_p6_c03]. In acoustic model experiments, training 10 separate models with different random initializations created sufficient diversity [P3_p5_c02]. Distillation used temperatures of [1, 2, 5, 10] and a relative weight of 0.5 on the cross-entropy for hard targets [P3_p5_c02]. More than 80% of the accuracy improvement from the 10-model ensemble transferred to the distilled model [P3_p5_c02].
